title: Facile electrochemical fabrication of Ag/Cu bi-metallic catalysts and the dependence of their selectivity for electrochemical CO2 reduction on the surface composition
abstract: Herein, bimetallic Ag/Cu nanowires (NWs) are prepared by electrochemical synthesis of Cu NWs and subsequent Ag galvanic displacement for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO. The delicate execution of the displacement fabricates bimetallic NWs that possess controlled surface composition. The surface composition of NW is precisely controlled by varying the displacement time, and it is revealed by numerical and experimental methods that the catalytic activity is closely affected by the composition. The surface coverage of Ag measured based on under potential deposition according to the displacement time ranges from 70% to 94.3%. An increase in the Ag surface composition results in an improvement in the CO Faradaic efficiency from 29.8% to 39.6% and a significant increase in CO partial current density compared with Cu NWs and Ag foil. Namely, the catalytic activity of Ag/Cu NWs is dependent on the Ag coverage, and is governed by scaling relation.

Facile electrochemical fabrication of Ag/Cu bi-metallic catalysts and the dependence of their selectivity for electrochemical CO2 reduction on the surface composition
Youngkeun Jeon a, Insoo Choi b,*, Jae Jeong Kim a,*
a School of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Institute of Chemical Process, Seoul National University, 1 Gwanak-ro, Gwanak-gu, Seoul 08826, South Korea b Division of Energy Engineering, Kangwon National University, 346 Jungang-ro, Gangwon-do, Samcheok 25913, South Korea
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Bi-metallic catalyst Copper Silver Nanowire Surface composition Carbon dioxide reduction Selectivity
A B S T R A C T
Herein, bimetallic Ag/Cu nanowires (NWs) are prepared by electrochemical synthesis of Cu NWs and subsequent Ag galvanic displacement for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO. The delicate execution of the displacement fabricates bimetallic NWs that possess controlled surface composition. The surface composition of NW is precisely controlled by varying the displacement time, and it is revealed by numerical and experimental methods that the catalytic activity is closely affected by the composition. The surface coverage of Ag measured based on under potential deposition according to the displacement time ranges from 70% to 94.3%. An increase in the Ag surface composition results in an improvement in the CO Faradaic efficiency from 29.8% to 39.6% and a significant increase in CO partial current density compared with Cu NWs and Ag foil. Namely, the catalytic activity of Ag/Cu NWs is dependent on the Ag coverage, and is governed by scaling relation.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Carbon dioxide (CO2) is one of the main green-house gases causing global warming. For this reason, many studies on ways to reduce the CO2 concentration in the air, such as CO2 capture, storage and conversion, have been conducted [1–3]. Among them, CO2 conversion using an electrochemical method has attracted attention due to the advantage that it can produce valuable carbon products, such as carbon monoxide (CO), formic acid (HCOOH) and methane (CH4) and so on under ambient pressure and temperature [4]. In particular, CO production by electrochemical conversion of CO2 is productive, because CO can be used as a component of syngas for the Fischer-Tropsch process [5]. To this end, many researchers have made an effort to find metal electrocatalysts with a good activity for CO2 reduction to CO and it was reported that gold (Au) and silver (Ag), among various metals, show excellent selectivity for CO production [6–8]. Although Au exhibits the best performance in terms of selectivity for CO production and overpotential, it has the major downside of a high cost. To apply metal electrocatalyst in large scale systems, cheaper metals than Au are required. From this point of view, Ag is regarded as a promising alternative metal catalyst.
Ag catalysts with various morphologies such as flat films, dendrites,
nanoparticles and nanowires (NWs) have been investigated for improving the performance of Ag catalysts for CO2 reduction [9–15]. Among various morphologies, NWs have been found to efficiently transport electrons due to their 1-D structure and expose many active sites due to their large surface area [16]. Chuhao Luan et al. used a nanomolding method based on an aluminum oxide template to fabricate Ag nanowire catalysts for CO2 reduction [17]. Ag catalysts with a nanowire structure fabricated by the nanomolding method displayed improved intrinsic activity and a large surface area. Minhyung Cho et al. synthesized Ag NWs by a modified polyol process, and then fabricated the Ag nanowire catalysts that control the H2/CO ratio by loading the synthesized Ag nanowire onto a macro-porous carbon sheet [18]. However, the fabrication methods of Ag NWs mentioned above require harsh conditions, such as the polyol method requiring over 100◦C [19].
Apart from different morphologies of catalysts, bimetallic catalysts for CO2 reduction have been researched [20–23]. Many researchers have synthesized metal alloys with the goal of improving catalytic performance with synergetic effect by alloy formation [24–26]. However, alloy formation requires harsh conditions, and a precise control of their composition is difficult. Instead of alloys, bimetallic catalysts can be fabricated with surface modifications such as chemical transformations and galvanic displacements on a sacrificial template [22,23]. With this

method, it is possible to reduce the loading amount of Ag. Moreover, the surface composition can be precisely controlled by surface modifications. When it comes to the performance of bimetallic electro-catalysts, the composition is an important factor. Accordingly, measurements of surface composition are essential when investigating the catalytic activity of bimetallic catalysts.
To facilely achieve the production of bimetallic NWs, electrochemical synthesis with template assistance and surface engineering was used. It was reported that electrochemical synthesis is one of the fabrication methods that can be used to obtain nanowire [27]. In addition, surfaces of NWs can be modified by surface engineering with electrochemical methods [23,27,28]. Through these fabrication designs, metal nanowire templates can be electrochemically fabricated under mild operating conditions, and then the surface of these metal NWs can be decorated with Ag using electrochemical reactions, such as electrodeposition and the galvanic displacement reaction, which results in the formation of a bimetallic nanowire. NWs fabricated using electrochemical methods have morphological advantages and a small loading amount of Ag, thereby leading to economic benefit and cost reduction.
In this work, bimetallic Ag/Cu NWs were fabricated by Ag galvanic displacement on Cu NWs for the electrochemical reduction of CO2. Cu NWs used for sacrificial templates were prepared using these three steps: anodization, calcination, and electrochemical reduction. The surface of Cu NWs was then tailored with Ag during galvanic displacement. The fabrication method can tune Ag coverage by changing the displacement time, thereby bimetallic Ag/Cu NWs with various Ag coverages were produced. We focus not only on the catalytic activity of Ag/Cu NWs for CO2 reduction, but also on the correlation between the varied surface composition and the selectivity of gaseous product: CO and H2. In fact, there have been many recent reports dealing with the effect of catalyst’s surface composition on the electrochemical reduction of CO2 [29,30]. Most of them have utilized X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), a physicochemical method, to characterize the surface composition. Although XPS is exclusively known for its surface sensitivity, its ability was manifested with flat surface rather than nanostructure [31]. We think that the surface characterization of nanowires would be even more precise if we employ a technique based on electrochemical reaction in the light of the fact that an electrochemical reaction occurs on the entire surface. In this context, we attempt to estimate the surface coverage of Ag with an electrochemical method, which includes the under potential deposition (UPD) of lead along with a numerical analysis to convolute stripping peaks of voltammogram for PbUPD on Ag and Cu, for an
accurate measurement, considering that samples have 3D nanowire network structure.

sections.heading: 2.1. Fabrication of Ag/Cu NWs
sections.text: Ag/Cu NWs were electrochemically prepared in a three-electrode system comprising of a counter electrode of Pt wire and a reference electrode of Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl). Firstly, Cu foil (thickness = 25 μm, Sigma Aldrich) was used as a working electrode. To synthesize Cu(OH)2 NWs, Cu foil was anodized in 2 M NaOH solution (98%, Daejung) of which the temperature was kept at 5◦C [32]. Sequential current densities of 5 mA/cm2 for 10 s, -5 mA/cm2 for 20 s and 3 mA/cm2 for 333 s were applied [27]. The second step was the calcination of Cu(OH)2 NWs to transform them into CuO NWs at air atmosphere at 250◦C for 1 hr. Next, CuO NWs were potentiostatically reduced to Cu by applying -1.2 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) in a 0.5 M NaOH (98%, Daejung). At last, Ag galvanic displacement was conducted to deposit Ag on Cu NWs. For Ag galvanic displacement, an electrolyte consisting of 0.1 M AgNO3 (99.9%, Kojima), 0.58 M (NH4)2SO4 (99%, Daejung) and 1.68 M NH4OH (25.0~28.0%, Daejung) was prepared. Cu NWs were dipped into the displacement electrolyte to obtain Ag_t s/Cu NWs (t denotes displacement time) for 5, 10, 15 and 20 s with 300 rpm.

sections.heading: 2.2. Material characterization
sections.text:
The morphologies of all prepared samples were analyzed using a field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, JSM-7600F, JEOL Ltd.) with the operating voltage of 3 kV. To analyze the bulk composition and distribution of Ag, energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) was conducted by FE-SEM. For an observation of the nanowire structure with a high magnification, a field emission transmission electron microscope (FE-TEM, JEM-F200, JEOL Ltd.) was utilized with the operating voltage of 200 kV. The high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) technique was used to conduct line scanning analysis, and the elemental mapping for Cu and Ag was performed in STEM mode. The crystal structures of the fabricated nanowire samples were analyzed with X-ray diffraction spectroscopy (XRD, D8-Advance, Bruker Miller Co.). The XRD analysis was conducted with an X-ray sources of Cu Kα radiation and θ-2θ configuration. The chemical states of nanowire samples were obtained using X-
Y. Jeon et al.
Thin Solid Films 726 (2021) 138674
ray photoelectron spectrometer (XPS, SIGMA PROBE, ThermoFisher Scientific) with monochromatic Al Kα X-ray source. The XPS analysis was performed in ultra-high vacuum (5 × 10− 8 Pa), and the binding energy scale of the spectra was referenced by Cls peak at 284.5 eV. Peak fitting was processed using a software (XPSpeak 4.1) with LorentzianGaussian function after Shirley-type background subtraction. Ion sputtering in the XPS analysis was not used in this study.

sections.heading: 2.3. Electrochemical analysis for the UPD of lead (Pb) on Cu and Ag/Cu NWs
sections.text: Pb UPD, which has been used as the electrochemical method for a surface characterization of various metals, was applied to estimate Ag coverage on nanowires in this study. Because the charge densities of PbUPD on Cu and Ag are reported, Ag coverage can be measured with both a result of cyclic voltammetry (CV) and charge density. Pb UPD on Cu and Ag/Cu NWs was conducted using cyclic voltammetry in a threeelectrode system consisting of Pt as a counter electrode and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as a reference electrode. The electrolyte for Pb UPD was made up of 0.5 mM Pb(ClO4)2 (98%, Sigma Aldrich) and 10 mM HClO4 (70%, Sigma Aldrich). This electrolyte was de-aerated with N2 gas for 30 min. Prior to CV analysis, -0.2 VSCE was applied to remove any metal oxides from the surface. CV for Pb UPD was carried out with a scan rate of 2 mV/s from open circuit potential to -0.5 VSCE.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical reduction of CO2
sections.text:
The electrolysis of CO2 was carried out using a potentiostat (EG&G, 263A, Princeton Applied Research) in an H-type cell segmented into cathode and anode parts by a proton exchange membrane (Nafion 211, Dupont). All experiments were conducted in a three-electrode cell system. A Pt gauze and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) were utilized as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. Synthesized Cu and Ag/Cu NWs were used as the working electrodes with a geometrical area of 2.5 cm2. 0.5 M KCl (99.5%, JUNSEI) was used as an anolyte. 0.5 M KHCO3 (99.5%, Daejung) was saturated with CO2 gas prior to electrolysis and used as a catholyte. CO2 gas was continuously purged into the catholyte with a rate of 10 ml/min during the electrochemical reduction of CO2. CO2 electrolysis was conducted for 30 min to analyze the catalytic activity of Ag/Cu NWs with varying reduction potential. The
concentration of products such as CO and H2 was measured by a gas chromatography (GC, HP 5890, Hewlett-Packard) system. Then, the Faradaic efficiency of CO and H2 was calculated based on both the measured concentrations of CO and H2 by GC and the total amount of the applied charge.

sections.heading: 3. Results
sections.text:
Fig. 1a–d show the surface SEM images of Cu(OH)2, CuO, Cu and Ag/ Cu NWs at each step during the fabrication of Ag/Cu NWs. The first step is the anodization of Cu foil to form Cu(OH)2 NWs. Prior to anodization, the Cu foil was electrochemically pretreated by applying oxidation and reduction currents sequentially to remove copper oxides [27]. Afterwards, the anodic current needed for the formation of Cu(OH)2 was applied on the pretreated Cu foils. It was reported that cupric ions can be electrochemically produced by applying adequate anodic current on Cu foil in alkaline solution and immediately react with hydroxide ions, so that copper hydroxide could be nucleated on the copper foil, and then deposited with nanowire structure [33]. After calcination at high temperature, the Cu(OH)2 NWs were transformed into CuO NWs with a slightly curved nanowire tip by dehydration. Subsequently CuO NWs were electrochemically reduced to Cu NWs. Cu NWs showed a rough surface, which was attributed to the removal of oxygen during the
Y. Jeon et al.
Thin Solid Films 726 (2021) 138674
electrochemical reduction of CuO to Cu. Fabricated Cu NWs had a length of 3.14 (±0.2) μm and a diameter of 91.9 (± 4.5) nm. At last, to decorate the Cu NWs with Ag, Ag galvanic displacement was conducted by immersing the prepared Cu NWs into the displacement electrolyte containing silver ions. During the galvanic displacement reaction, Ag (NH3)2+ present in the electrolyte is electrochemically reduced to Ag, while the Cu NWs are electrochemically oxidized to Cu ions, so that Ag covers the surface of the Cu NWs. Fig. 1d exhibits that the nanowire structure was well maintained after galvanic displacement and that an increase in the diameter of Ag/Cu NWs (130 (± 10) nm) was observed compared with that of Cu NWs. It was found from this observation that additional Ag layer was formed on Cu nanowire with well-maintained nanowire structure.
To observe the structure of the prepared Cu and Ag/Cu NWs under a high magnification, TEM images and EDS elemental mapping results were obtained as shown in Fig. 2. Fig. 2a indicates the TEM image of Cu NWs, which shows that the Cu NWs consisted of nanoparticles. It was reported that an oriented aggregation of Cu(OH)2 nanoparticles can lead to the formation of Cu(OH)2 NW during anodization [33]. Because Cu (OH)2 was an original component of the NWs, the structure of the stacked nanoparticles was reflected to the Cu NW. TEM images of Ag_5 s/Cu NWs are shown in Fig. 2b and indicate that the core is brighter than the shells of NWs, which means that empty sites could exist in the core region. Fig. 2c–f of a bright-field TEM image and elemental mapping results clearly demonstrate that there were pores in the core region. Furthermore, the results of a line scan analysis in the radial direction, which are presented in Fig. 2g reveal that as the detection point went from a shell to a core, the signal of Cu increased and decreased, and then increased again at a certain point to the maximum value. Considering
Y. Jeon et al.
Thin Solid Films 726 (2021) 138674
this result, it was concluded that Cu-rich core exists in the center of nanowire, and that pores were formed between the core and shell layers. The results of TEM analysis was similar to that of other studies involving dissolution process of metal in core of nanostructures [34–36]. The formation of pores in the nanowires can be explained using two different points of view. First, a factor affecting the formation of pores is pitting corrosion of Cu that can actively occur due to the nitrate ions contained in the displacement electrolyte [37]. Second, a Kirkendall void is produced by the difference in the diffusion rates between Cu and Ag [38–40]. Accordingly, fabricated Ag/Cu NWs have a structure containing pores between the Cu-rich core in the center and shell layer consisting of Ag and Cu.
The crystal structures of Cu(OH)2, CuO, Cu and Ag_5 s/Cu NWs were investigated by X-ray diffraction, as shown in Fig. 3. It is clear from Fig. 3 that the main materials, such as Cu(OH)2, CuO, Cu and Ag, were formed and transformed at each step. Three diffraction peaks appeared for all samples; 43.3◦, 50.4◦ and 74.1◦ corresponding to Cu(111), (200) and (220), respectively. The diffraction peaks for Cu in the XRD patterns
of Cu(OH)2 and CuO NWs were from the Cu foil substrate. For the Cu and Ag_5 s/Cu NWs, although the characteristic peaks for Cu were mainly affected by the Cu foil, the existence of Cu in nanowire could contribute to those. The XRD pattern of Cu(OH)2 displays 6 broad diffraction peaks identified to be from an orthorhombic structure of Cu(OH)2. The diffraction peaks at 35.5◦ and 38.9◦ of the spectra of the CuO NWs corresponded to the (111) and (200) lattice planes of a monoclinic CuO. Moreover, the peaks observed at 42.3◦ and 61.3◦ were related to (200) and (220) of cubic Cu2O, respectively. The formation of Cu2O was due to oxidation of an exposed Cu foil on the bottom during calcination in 250◦C. After the electrochemical reduction of CuO NWs, only the three characteristic peaks of Cu mentioned above were detected, which indicates the fabrication of Cu NWs. Ag(111), Ag(200), Ag(220) and Ag (311) peaks at 38.1◦, 44.2◦, 64.4◦ and 77.4◦ were detected in the diffraction pattern of Ag_5 s/Cu NWs. In addition, the appearance of the shoulder peak and shift of characteristic peaks for Cu and Ag in XRD pattern, which could be the sign for alloy phase formation were not observed. This result was supported by results of XPS analysis shown in Fig. 4. The Ag3d and Cu2p peaks of Ag_5 s/Cu NWs displayed the binding energies assigned to metallic Ag0 and Cu0, respectively. Although XPS spectrum of Cu2p also indicated peaks corresponded to Cu2+ due to formation of copper hydroxide during displacement process in alkaline solution, peaks of Cu0 and Ag0 were well-matched with the binding energy of pure metals, and their shifts were not observed, which meant that Cu-Ag alloy was not formed after displacement. Accordingly, it is obvious that pure Cu and Ag were not alloyed, but mixed in the Ag/Cu NWs in the light of the results of XRD and XPS analyses.
Ag galvanic displacement was conducted for a prolonged time of 10,15 and 20 s to control the Ag content. Fig. 5a–d exhibit a wellmaintained nanowire structure after displacement for these prolonged durations. Also, SEM images in Fig. 5e and f indicate the porous interior structure explained with TEM images (Fig. 2) even after Ag displacement for 20 s, which means that all the prepared samples have the same structure. With the Ag galvanic displacement for 20 s, the diameter of the NWs was increased to 290 (± 50) nm. EDS mapping images shown in Fig. 6a–h indicate that Ag was uniformly deposited on the NWs for all prepared samples, which meant the formation of Ag/Cu NWs. The signal of Ag existing on the bottom of NWs and the empty space between entangled NWs was weaker than that on the top of NWs. This was attributed to the relatively difficult mass transfer of Ag ions toward these sites, despite applying 300 rpm, because the NWs were stood at an angle and entangled with each other. [15,41]. In addition, Ag composition measured by EDS analysis ranged from 63.9% to 95.0% with increasing Ag displacement time. This result means that increasing displacement time led to an increase in the deposited and consumed amount of Ag and Cu, respectively, during displacement, thereby controlling the Ag content of the nanowire samples.
The Ag surface composition was estimated from the electrochemical method. Although a change in the Ag bulk composition was measured according to displacement time, investigation of the surface composition was essential, because the electrochemical reduction of CO2 occurs on the surface of the NWs. To estimate the Ag coverage with displacement time, the electrochemical method with Pb UPD on Ag/Cu NWs was applied. It was reported that Pb UPD can take place on the both, the Cu and Ag, and the charge densities associated with Pb UPD on Ag and Cu were 260 and 310 μC/cm2, respectively [42–44]. This property of Pb UPD has been used to calculate the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) of Cu and Ag in many studies [45]. CV results shown in Fig. 6a show the cathodic and anodic peaks for Pb UPD on Ag and Cu rotating disk electrode (RDE) in the potential region between -0.25 VSCE and -0.35 VSCE. In addition, the current peaks for Pb bulk deposition and Pbbulk deposition stripping appeared at -0.5 VSCE and -0.46 VSCE, respectively. It was found that the peak potentials for Pb UPD and PbUPD stripping on Ag RDE were significantly close to those on Cu RDE. This feature was reflected on the voltammograms of all prepared NWs samples. The CV results for Pb UPD according to displacement time are

presented in Fig. 6b. During the forward scan, the cathodic peak appeared at -0.3 VSCE corresponding to Pb UPD. As the potential moved backwards, a PbUPD stripping peak in the anodic region was observed at -0.25 VSCE. Because the peak positions for Pb UPD and PbUPD stripping on Ag and Cu were similar, as shown in Fig. 6a, the peaks observed in Fig. 6b are the result from the contributions of both, Ag and Cu. In Fig. 6b, charge balance calculated by using charging current as a base line in forward and backward scans was well matched. Also, CV results indicated a cathodic current density for Pb bulk deposition during the forward scan and an anodic current density for Pbbulk deposition stripping during the backward scan in the potential region between -0.45 VSCE and -0.5 VSCE.
For an estimation of Ag coverage of the Ag/Cu_x NWs, the PbUPD stripping peaks had to be deconvoluted by two kinds of peaks; PbUPD stripping on Ag, PbUPD stripping on Cu. As PbUPD stripping on Ag occurred at a more negative potential than for Cu, as shown in Fig. 6a, the order of the two peaks could be determined. To conduct the fitting of the PbUPD stripping peak, the i-E curve equation for absorbed monolayers with irreversible reaction was applied [46]. The reversibility of Pb UPD on Ag and Cu was determined by the difference value between EUPD and EStripping (E means the peak potential of Pb UPD and PbUPD stripping current density). Whether this value is higher or lower than 57/n (n=2, the number of electrons involved in the corresponding reaction) mV is a barometer to judge the reversibility of an electrochemical reaction. Fig. 6a showed a higher peak potential difference between Pb UPD and PbUPD stripping than 57/n (n=2) mV for both, Ag and Cu, which means that the reaction on both, Ag and Cu was an irreversible process. Fitting results are exhibited in Fig. 7. It was found that the Ag and Cu contributions were enhanced and reduced, respectively, with increasing displacement time. The Ag coverage calculated on the basis of the fitting results was plotted as a function of the displacement time in Fig. 6c. As a result, Ag coverage changed from 70% to 94.3%, as the displacement time increased from 5 s to 20 s. As the calculated Ag coverage was compared with the Ag content measured by SEM-EDS analysis, there was a gap between the Ag coverage and Ag content, which diminished with longer displacement time. For a shorter displacement time, a Cu-rich core in the center was clearly observed in the TEM image
(Fig. 2c), which resulted in the underestimation of bulk Ag composition. However, as the displacement proceeded for a longer time, more Cu atoms from Cu-rich core in the center diffused out and were consumed, thereby decreasing amount of Cu in the inner space. This phenomena resulted in a narrow gap between the Ag coverage and Ag content measured from EDS for long displacements. Based on the two composition analyses, it is remarkable that control of displacement time can change the composition of Ag for Ag/Cu NWs, and a nanowire for which the surface consisted of almost only Ag can be obtained. Finally, we found that adjusting the displacement time can cause changes in the surface coverage by Ag on NWs.
To demonstrate the relation between the displacement time and a catalytic activity of the Ag/Cu NWs, a catalytic performance for an electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO was measured. First of all, the effect of the reduction potential on the catalytic activity was investigated with Ag_5 s/Cu NWs, as shown in Fig. 8. Fig. 8a depicts the CO and H2 Faradaic efficiency depending on the applied potential, and shows optimum point for the CO Faradaic efficiency. For Ag_5 s/Cu NWs, -0.82 VRHE exhibited the best performance among various reduction potentials. For the CO/H2 ratio, there is no big difference in the potential region from -0.62 VRHE to- 0.82 VRHE. However, in the potential region below -0.82 VRHE it dramatically decreased to the value of 0.57 shown in Fig. 8b. As the potential was shifted toward a negative value, the hydrogen evolution reaction became more active than the formation of CO (blue line in Fig. 8a) and the conversion of CO2 to unknown liquid products was enhanced, as shown in Fig. 8c displaying CO fraction among the reduced products from CO2 electrolysis, which is the value of produced CO amount divided by total amount of product from CO2 reduction, according to applied potential [47–49]. For this reason, the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO using the prepared sample is most efficient at -0.82 VRHE.
Fig. 9 demonstrates the change in catalytic activity for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO according to the Ag coverage at -0.82 VRHE. The CO Faradaic efficiency, CO partial current density and CO/H2 ratio of Ag_5 s/Cu NWs with 70% Ag coverage were much higher than that of the Cu NWs, which can be explained by the fact that Cu can generate various products from CO2 and the surface of the Cu NWs were

tailored with Ag which exhibits a high catalytic activity for CO production. Compared with Ag foil, Ag/Cu NWs indicated a 5-8.5 times higher CO partial current density due to the morphological advantage of the nanowire structure. In addition, as the Ag coverage increased, both, CO Faradaic efficiency and partial current density were enhanced. With increasing the Ag coverage from 70% s to 94.3%, the CO Faradaic efficiency was improved from 29.8% to 39.6% and the CO partial current density increased 1.75 times. Especially, the CO Faradaic efficiency of Ag_20 s/Cu NWs is 1.3 times higher than that in the research conducted by Ahn’s group, which studied the same component as that of this study and applied similar electrochemical process to fabricate a electrocatalyst, but it has a different nanostructure [22]. Moreover, when the catalytic activity of Ag_20 s/Cu NWs with 94.3% Ag coverage was compared with that of the Cu NWs and Ag foil, the CO partial current density of the Ag_20 s/Cu NWs with 94.3% Ag coverage was 24.7 and 8.5 times higher than for the Cu NWs and Ag foil, respectively. As a result, tuning the Ag coverage can significantly affect the catalytic activity of Ag/Cu NWs for CO2 reduction to CO. In other words, the
catalytic activity for CO production was dependent on the Ag coverage of the surface of the NWs. Namely, the increase in Ag coverage significantly contributed to the improvement in catalytic activity, due to the presence of Ag atoms which can promote CO production during the electrochemical reduction of CO2 owing to their high selectivity for this compound.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
The preparation of Ag/Cu NWs proceeded by the electrochemical methods of anodization and galvanic displacement. The sequential steps of anodization, calcination and electrochemical reduction led to the formation and transformation of Cu(OH)2 to Cu NWs. The surface of Cu NWs prepared from this method was tailored with Ag using the galvanic displacement reaction. The result of the TEM analysis showed that the structure of Ag/Cu NWs contained pores between Cu-rich core in the center and the shell layer. The surface composition of the prepared bimetallic Ag/Cu NWs was measured according to displacement time, and the surface coverage of Ag estimated by the Pb UPD method ranged from 70 % to 94.3%. For CO2 electrolysis, -0.82 VRHE was the optimum reduction potential on the basis of the catalytic activity of Ag/Cu NWs for the conversion of CO2 to CO. In addition, both CO Faradaic efficiency and CO partial current density for Ag/Cu NWs were significantly enhanced compared to Cu NWs. With increasing the Ag coverage, the CO Faradaic efficiency was improved from 29.8% to 39.6%. In addition, the CO partial current density of Ag_20 s/Cu NWs was 24.7 and 8.5 times higher than for Cu NWs and Ag foil, respectively. In conclusion, the catalytic activity of bimetallic Ag/Cu NWs significantly depended on the Ag coverage of the NWs.Credit Author Statement
